video_title: How to kill your SaaS: what we learned replacing a $43K/yr tool with AI agents
gist: Latent Space/AI Engineer ran a 'Kill My SAS' contest to replace a $43K/yr event-software vendor; 72 teams submitted agent-built clones, and an events team judged them. Findings: automated AI judges correlate poorly with humans, builders mix Claude and Codex, and maintenance/accountability is the real remaining SaaS moat.

insights.claim: Latent Space/AI Engineer was quoted $43,000 a year by event-software vendor Session Board for four events, while using only about a third of the bundle with no discount for unused parts.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Per-seat/bundle pricing on mid-tier vertical SaaS is the clearest target for AI-agent replacement.
insights.quote: they quoted us $43,000 a year for four events

insights.claim: The host reversed a founding-contract rule banning internal software builds because agents are now good enough for personalized software, putting a $10,000 prize and up to $500 token reimbursement per serious builder behind the test.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: A sophisticated buyer abandoning 'not invented here' discipline signals a real shift in build-vs-buy economics.
insights.quote: I think agents are finally good enough for us to have personalized software

insights.claim: Cloning a piece of mid-tier software is estimated at roughly $1,000 in tokens/subscriptions plus about $10,000 of AI engineering expertise, versus a $43K/yr license, in exchange for owning maintenance.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Payback on custom builds can be under one year for mid-tier SaaS; the residual cost shifts to maintenance headcount.

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf vendors take 3 to 6 months or never to ship a requested change, whereas the in-house team now gets minute-level turnaround on bug reports and feature requests.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Iteration speed, not just price, is the wedge against incumbent vertical SaaS.
insights.quote: it often takes something like 3 months to 6 months or never for them to actually ship something

insights.claim: The host expects savings to fund software improvements the team could never afford before, rather than just cutting cost; non-engineers (designers, ops, domain experts) are among the heaviest coders on the team.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Domain experts directly steering coding agents is the labor-model change behind SaaS displacement.

themes.theme: Why SaaS is not simply dead

insights.claim: Cloning something that looks like it works is the easy part; the hard part is ongoing ownership: bug reports, 2 a.m. fixes and accountability, as when the team threw a dozen Codex agents at a program right before launch.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Vendors' durable moat is accountability and maintenance, so the killable SaaS is the poorly maintained, poorly loved kind.
insights.quote: If you break it, you own it

insights.claim: The events head of ops cited vendor support chains ending in 'refresh your cache' as an accountability failure and said she wants someone able to go in and fix errors immediately rather than depend on a vendor.
insights.speaker: Kelsey (head of ops, AI Engineer)
insights.so_what: Poor vendor support responsiveness is a churn driver that custom builds exploit.
insights.quote: I can't ask someone who's like you know at a multi-million dollar company to refresh their cash because something we did broke.

insights.claim: Piecemeal, hodge-podged integrations (registration to sponsor portal to schedule) are a pain the team wants fixed with an all-in-one system, which off-the-shelf tools fail to give.
insights.speaker: Kelsey (head of ops, AI Engineer)
insights.so_what: Integrated, workflow-spanning software is a better target than single-feature clones.

insights.claim: Agents are making maintenance and customization of in-house software far more feasible than 12 months ago, so the build-and-own trade is not a net negative.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Lower maintenance cost is the variable that flips build-vs-buy.

insights.claim: Of 72 submissions, 56 apps were run through an automated Claude-driven eval of 20 user-flow scenarios, 40 had enough coverage to rank, and the top seven landed within 2.3 points of each other, which is saturation.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Automated evals saturate quickly and cannot separate the top tier.

insights.claim: AI judge scores correlated poorly with human judgments: six of the AI judge's top 10 were rated weak by the events team, and the overall winner ranked 19th on the AI judge leaderboard.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: LLM-judge leaderboards are a weak proxy for real buyer satisfaction; human taste evals still decide.
insights.quote: our winner was 19th on the own on the AI judge leaderboard

insights.claim: Hill-climbing against a published automated eval is a useful bootstrap, but builders then duplicated features without connecting them because they did not dogfood the integrated app.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Per-feature evals miss integration quality, the area where agent-built apps fail.

insights.claim: The three hardest items for submissions were multi-portal support, drag-and-drop scheduling without double-booking, and adding invited speakers without going through the CFP form; none were well specified in the docs and were only found by using the product like a real user.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Unwritten workflow knowledge is the real moat of vertical software and the part agents miss without real-user testing.

insights.claim: The median public repo was 91,000 lines of code, agents ran for days, Claude Code and Codex were tied in usage, and 40 of 66 submissions used both; all three finalists used GPT, as did 50 of the other 66.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: There is no single-vendor lock for coding agents; builders mix model families, limiting any one lab's pricing power.

insights.claim: Three multi-model patterns emerged: a smart model plans while a cheaper model writes code, one model builds while another (the better browser driver, currently GPT/Codex) checks, and no model approves its own work.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Cross-model verification is an emerging best practice and a demand driver for multiple frontier subscriptions.

insights.claim: Agents are easier on their own work than on others' work, so one finalist ran separate Claude and Codex teams where neither could merge until the other verified.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Independent verification layers (on-policy versus off-policy) are a design requirement for autonomous coding pipelines.

insights.claim: Finalists spent most effort before prompting: Marco spent about 8 hours planning schema, business logic and pseudo code, then let an LLM build for 2 to 3 hours; Yazin crawled the vendor's help site with firecrawl; Valentin had Codex map every flow from videos.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Spec and context quality, not clever prompting, determines agent output; research tooling (crawlers, video-to-spec) is the real workflow.
insights.quote: the prompt was almost the last step that you sort of lead up to

insights.claim: The agent was very good at building but quite bad at noticing UX issues, for example a headshot upload that saved a photo somewhere the public speaker page never read.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Agent-built apps need human dogfooding; integration bugs between independently coded features are a recurring failure mode.

insights.claim: Finalist Valentin applied a five-minute test: if the product cannot be navigated smoothly in five minutes, context is missing and the whole process is redone rather than patched manually; he packaged his guardrails as an open-source GitHub template.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Reusable repo templates and redo-from-context loops are becoming the unit of agent engineering practice.

insights.claim: Marco used Convex and Next.js as his preferred stack because Convex gives a real-time database that is performant without much work.
insights.speaker: Marco
insights.so_what: Opinionated, agent-friendly backend stacks (Convex) may gain adoption among agent-driven builders.

insights.claim: Winners were chosen on taste and independent UX judgment: the contest let people deviate from the spec, partly as a hiring exercise for people who can code with taste, and an unrequested all-in-one deliverables page won praise from the events team.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: As cloning becomes cheap, product taste is the scarce differentiator.

insights.claim: Five apps cleared the bar to adopt or seriously consider, 12 more had ideas worth stealing, and AI Engineer plans to run 2027 events on a mix of Open Roster and Conferencer, all open source.
insights.speaker: Swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Open-source agent-built alternatives can credibly displace a $43K/yr incumbent in a real production deployment.
